L0: # Self-Distillation Amplifies Regularization in Hilbert Space
L1: 
L2: Hossein Mobahi, Mehrdad Farajtabar, Peter L. Bartlett
L3: 
L4: cite0†Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020) L5: 
L6: cite1†AuthorFeedback cite2†Bibtex cite3†MetaReview cite4†Paper cite5†Review cite6†Supplemental L7: ## Abstract
L8: Knowledge distillation introduced in the deep learning context is a method to transfer knowledge from one architecture to another. In particular, when the architectures are identical, this is called self-distillation. The idea is to feed in predictions of the trained model as new target values for retraining (and iterate this loop possibly a few times). It has been empirically observed that the self-distilled model often achieves higher accuracy on held out data.
L9: Why this happens, however, has been a mystery: the self-distillation dynamics does not receive any new information about the task and solely evolves by looping over training. To the best of our knowledge, there is no rigorous understanding of why this happens. This work provides the first theoretical analysis of self-distillation. We focus on fitting a nonlinear function to training data, where the model space is Hilbert space and fitting is subject to L2 regularization in this function space.
L10: We show that self-distillation iterations modify regularization by progressively limiting the number of basis functions that can be used to represent the solution. This implies (as we also verify empirically) that while a few rounds of self-distillation may reduce over-fitting, further rounds may lead to under-fitting and thus worse performance.

L11@P0: Abstract
L12@P0: Knowledge distillation is classically a procedure where a neural network is trained
L13@P0: on the output of another network along with the original targets in order to transfer
L14@P0: knowledge between the architectures. The special case of self-distillation, where
L15@P0: the network architectures are identical, has been observed to improve generalization
L16@P0: accuracy. In this paper, we consider an iterative variant of self-distillation in a
L17@P0: kernel regression setting, in which successive steps incorporate both model outputs
L18@P0: and the ground-truth targets. This allows us to provide the first theoretical results
L19@P0: on the importance of using the weighted ground-truth targets in self-distillation.
L20@P0: Our focus is on fitting nonlinear functions to training data with a weighted mean
L21@P0: square error objective function suitable for distillation, subject to `2 regularization
L22@P0: of the model parameters. We show that any such function obtained with selfdistillation can be calculated directly as a function of the initial fit, and that infinite
L23@P0: distillation steps yields the same optimization problem as the original with amplified
L24@P0: regularization. Furthermore, we provide a closed form solution for the optimal
L25@P0: choice of weighting parameter at each step, and show how to efficiently estimate this
L26@P0: weighting parameter for deep learning and significantly reduce the computational
L27@P0: requirements compared to a grid search.
L28@P0: 1 Introduction
L29@P0: Knowledge distillation, most commonly known from Hinton et al. (2015), is a procedure to transfer
L30@P0: knowledge from one neural network (teacher) to another neural network (student).1 Often the student
L31@P0: has fewer parameters than the teacher, and the procedure can be seen as a model compression
L32@P0: technique. Originally, the distillation procedure achieves the knowledge transfer by training the
L33@P0: student network using the original training targets, denoted as ground-truth targets, as well as a
L34@P0: softened distribution of logits from the (already trained and fixed) teacher network.2 Since the
L35@P0: popularization of knowledge distillation by Hinton et al. (2015), the idea of knowledge distillation
L36@P0: has been extended to a variety of settings.3 This paper will focus on the special case where the teacher
L37@P0: and student are of identical architecture, called self-distillation, and where the aim is to improve
L38@P0: predictive performance, rather than compressing the model.
L39@P0: The idea of self-distillation is to use outputs from a trained model together with the original targets as
L40@P0: new targets for retraining the same model from scratch. We refer to this as one step of self-distillation,
L41@P0: and one can iterate this procedure for multiple distillation steps (see Figure 1). Empirically, it
L42@P0: has been shown that this procedure often generalizes better than the model trained merely on the
L43@P0: 1Often knowledge distillation is also referred to under the name Teacher-Student learning.
L44@P0: 2We will refer to the weighted outputs of the penultimate layer, i.e. pre-activation of the last layer, as logits.

L46@P0: See Section 2 for a brief overview, or see Wang and Yoon (2020) for a more exhaustive survey
L47@P0-1: 35th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2021).original targets, and achieves higher predictive performance on validation data, despite no additional
L48@P1: information being provided during training (Furlanello et al., 2018; Ahn et al., 2019; Yang et al.,
L49@P1: 2018).

L53@P1: ). See Section 3 for details.
L54@P1: Modern deep neural networks are often trained in the over-parameterized regime, where the amount
L55@P1: of trainable parameters highly exceed the amount of training samples. Under simple first-order
L56@P1: methods such as gradient descent, such large networks can fit any target, but in order to generalize
L57@P1: well, such overfitting is usually undesirable (Zhang et al., 2017; Nakkiran et al., 2020). Thus, some
L58@P1: type of regularization is typically imposed during training, in order to avoid overfitting. A common
L59@P1: choice is to add an `2-regularization4term to our objective function, which has been shown to
L60@P1: perform comparably to early-stopping gradient descent training (Yao et al., 2007). However, in the
L61@P1: theoretical study of the over-parameterized regime, regularization is often overlooked, but recent
L62@P1: results have shown a connection between wide neural networks and kernel ridge regression through
L63@P1: the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) (Lee et al., 2019, 2020; Hu et al., 2019). We briefly elaborate on
L64@P1: this connection in Section D, which motivates our problem setup and connection to deep learning in
L65@P1: Section 5.
L66@P1: Our Contributions Through a theoretical analysis we show that
L67@P1: • the solution at any distillation step can easily be calculated as a function of the initial fit,
L68@P1: and infinitely many steps of self-distillation (with fixed distillation weight) correspond to
L69@P1: solving the usual kernel ridge regression problem with a specific amplified regularization
L70@P1: parameter when the distillation weight is non-zero,
L71@P1: • for fixed distillation weights, self-distillation amplifies the regularization at each distillation
L72@P1: step, and the ground-truth targets dampen the sparsification and regularization of the selfdistilled solutions, ensuring non-zero solutions for any number of distillation steps,
L73@P1: • the optimal distillation weight has a closed form solution for kernel ridge regression, and
L74@P1: can be estimated efficiently for neural networks compared to a grid search.
L75@P1: Proofs of all our results can be found in Supplementary Material A, and code to reproduce
L76@P1: our illustrative example in Section 4.5. Experimental results in Section B can be found at
L77@P1: github.com/Kennethborup/self_distillation.
L78@P1: 2 Related Work
L79@P1: The idea of knowledge distillation dates back to Bucila et al. (2006), and was later brought to the deep
L80@P1: learning setting by Ba and Caruana (2014) and more recently popularized by Hinton et al. (2015) in
L81@P1: the context of compressing neural networks. Since the original formulation, various extensions have
L82@P1: been proposed. Some approaches focus on matching the teacher and student models on statistics other
L83@P1: than the distribution of the logits, such as intermediate representations (Romero et al., 2015), spacial
L84@P1: attention maps (Zagoruyko and Komodakis, 2019), Jacobians (Srinivas and Fleuret, 2018), Gram
L85@P1: matrices (Yim et al., 2017), or relational information between teacher outputs (Park et al., 2019).
L86@P1: Other extensions focus on developing the transfer procedure, such as self-distillation (Furlanello
L87@P1: et al., 2018), data-free distillation (Lopes et al., 2017; Nayak et al., 2019; Micaelli and Storkey, 2019;
L88@P1: Chen et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2019), data distillation (Radosavovic et al., 2018), residual knowledge
L89@P1: distillation (Gao et al., 2020), online distillation (Anil et al., 2018) or contrastive distillation (Ahn
L90@P1: et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2020a).
L91@P1: 4With slight differences, `2 regularization is often referred to as weight decay and ridge regularization in
L92@P1: deep learning and statistical learning literature, respectively. See e.g. Loshchilov and Hutter (2019) for details.
L93@P1-2: 2The practical benefits of knowledge distillation have been proven countless of times in a variety of
L94@P2: settings, but the theoretical justification for knowledge distillation is still highly absent. Hinton et al.
L95@P2: (2015) conjecture that the success of knowledge distillation should be attributed to the transfer of dark
L96@P2: knowledge (e.g. inter-class relationships revealed in the soft labels). Müller et al. (2019); Tang et al.
L97@P2: (2020) support this conjecture, and argue that knowledge distillation is similar to performing adaptive
L98@P2: label smoothing weighted by the teacher’s confidence in the predictions. Dong et al. (2019) show
L99@P2: the importance of early stopping when training over-parameterized neural networks for distillation
L100@P2: purposes by arguing that neural networks tend to fit informative and simple patterns faster than
L101@P2: noisy signals, and knowledge distillation utilizes these simple patterns for knowledge transfer. Abnar
L102@P2: et al. (2020) empirically investigate how knowledge distillation can transfer inductive biases between
L103@P2: student and teacher models, and Gotmare et al. (2019) empirically shows how the dark knowledge
L104@P2: shared by the teacher mainly is disbursed to some of the deepest layers of the teacher.
L105@P2: To the best of our knowledge, few papers investigate knowledge distillation from a rigorous theoretical
L106@P2: point of view, and those that do, do so with strong assumptions on the setting. Phuong and Lampert
L107@P2: (2019) ignore the ground-truth targets during distillation and furthermore assume linear models.
L108@P2: Mobahi et al. (2020) investigate self-distillation in a Hilbert space setting with kernel ridge regression
L109@P2: models where the teacher is trained on the ground-truth targets, and the student (and subsequent
L110@P2: iterations) is only trained on the predictions from the teacher without access to the ground-truth
L111@P2: targets. They show that self-distillation progressively limits the number of basis functions used to
L112@P2: represent the solutions, thus eventually causing the solutions to underfit. In this paper, we build on
L113@P2: the theoretical results of Mobahi et al. (2020), but we include the weighted ground-truth targets in
L114@P2: the self-distillation procedure, where we allow the weight to depend on the self-distillation step, and
L115@P2: show how this drastically affects the behavior and effect of self-distillation.5
